quick.summary: Why broad communication causes arguments, and how to involve the right people.
quick.takeaway: Builders get a vote on the plan. Users just get a schedule.

beats.line: I sent the database migration plan to forty people. Why is everyone arguing?
You invited the customers into the kitchen.
The chef cooks. The waiter serves. The customer eats.
If customers season the soup, dinner is ruined.
So I should not ask everyone for their thoughts?
Right. We separate the roles. We call this a responsibility assignment matrix.
Can I just say who does what?
That works well. Let us use who does what.
Builders get a vote. Users just get a schedule.
I will ask the engineers for feedback, and just tell the analysts the date.
That is exactly how you serve a good meal.

quiz.question: You are upgrading the data warehouse. Who should approve the detailed steps?
quiz.explanation: Only the builders need a vote on the plan. Users only need to know when the system will be offline.

quiz.question: Asking more people for feedback always leads to a better project plan.
quiz.explanation: Asking too many people creates confusion. You should strictly define who builds, who approves, and who is just informed.
